entities.summary:
Shepseskare, also known as Shepseskara, reigned briefly as an Ancient Egyptian pharaoh during the mid-25th century BCE, typically identified as the fourth or fifth ruler of the Fifth Dynasty (c. 2494–2345 BCE) in the Old Kingdom period. His ephemeral rule, estimated at only a few months, is attested by a royal seal discovered at Abusir and a mention in the Saqqara King List, placing him within the lineage of pharaohs who succeeded Userkaf and Sahure, and preceded Neferirkare Kakai. While his existence is archaeologically confirmed, Shepseskare's reign represents a fleeting moment of dynastic transition, offering limited insight into the political and administrative structures of a highly centralized state at the zenith of pyramid building.

The primary material evidence for Shepseskare's reign is an unfinished pyramid complex located in the royal necropolis of Abusir, a site that served as the primary burial ground for Fifth Dynasty pharaohs. Excavations reveal that construction on his pyramid ceased after only a few weeks, with the foundational layers barely established, suggesting an abrupt end to his rule—possibly due to a short lifespan or usurpation. This abandoned project, characterized by a large rectangular trench intended for the pyramid's core and a surrounding enclosure wall, stands in stark contrast to the grand, completed monuments of his dynastic predecessors and successors, underscoring the brevity and perhaps instability of his time on the throne.
